Then there is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Everyone takes it for granted that he is Mr. Socialist. Then there is the hon, member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher); and there is no argument about it, he is Mr. Capitalist. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) will of course be known as Mr. Professor. There is no denying that. The hon, member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) is without doubt Mr. Independent. There is one other gentleman that I dare not leave out. He was a former member of this house. I refer to the present premier of Saskatchewan. His name will surely go down in history as Mr. Politician. He is the biggest politician on the North American continent, bar none. Here is the description of these various gentlemen that I give. I offer the descriptions with no malice whatsoever, Mr. Speaker. No doubt as time goes on I shall get a proper description of myself.
I should be getting pretty close to the end of what I did not have to say. I wish to make one or two more remarks and then I shall be thankful for your consideration. The newspapers are playing a great part in the history of this country. So far as the opposition members are concerned, seldom do they speak without holding up a clipping from some newspaper in Canada, describing what in the editor's opinion should be done. If the newspapers of this country are running the country-and they are because sooner or later we are going to do what they say-if that is so, then I suggest that they should be represented in this House of Commons. I think they would be able to give great service to the people of this country and to the House of Commons if they displaced some of the members of the opposition, because they have been awfully weak in their arguments, and I am sure that some of the editors would be much more helpful than what we hear in this house day after day.
Some of these newspapers might be able to give assistance to the government side of the house, because it would eliminate a lot of this misquoting and a lot of the instructions to newspaper reporters. This is the instruction that is given to them: "We are not so much interested in what he says; go out and get a story". If we had a much more extensive representation in the House of Commons some of that would be eliminated.
Then, if we had representation from newspapers on the government side of the house there would be the necessity of having parliamentary assistants and we are surrounded with likely candidates over here. The hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. McWilliam), the editor of the North Shore
The Address-Mr. Studer Leader, the hon. member for Durham (Mr. James), the editor of the Bowmanville Statesman, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray), the editor of the Alaska Highway, and the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. McLean), the editor of the Huron Expositor, would all fit the bill. We would have lots of assistance in the House of Commons in regard to keeping the record straight.
If they are to displace anyone in opposition I would suggest that they be displaced by the editor of the Montreal Gazette, the editor of the Ottawa Journal, the editor of the Globe and Mail, the editor of the Vancouver Province, the editor of the Winnipeg Tribune and the editor of the Halifax Herald. If our socialist friends over there need some assistance I would nominate the editor of the Saskatchewan Commonwealth. He has the keenest one-track mind in Canada.
Since we are living in a troubled world perhaps we should not be prone to levity. We are living in a world where, as everyone knows, it is considered that might is right. In Canada we have adopted the philosophy that only right makes might. Therefore we are living in a world in which there are these two philosophies of life. As the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) and the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald) said yesterday in their well delivered speeches, the real danger that confronts us is an enemy who is ruthless and who will stop at nothing to achieve his purposes.
In closing I should like to say that in my opinion the system that the enemy is using at the present time to undermine the nations of the world is both physical and psychological. That is, he appeals to the hunger that is in people. He appeals to their suffering and then to their spirit. There has been a concerted effort during a great number of years by these people who control the Kremlin, and hope to control the world, to destroy people's minds. As I said, their appeal is both physical and psychological. That is true especially in regard to the different races of the world.
As we know it today, the white race is outnumbered seven to one. That is, there are seven coloured people to every white person in the world today. I believe the Kremlin is making an appeal to these coloured people all over the world. They are filling them with the doctrine that the white people have dominated them and exploited them throughout the centuries. They tell them that their enemies are the white people of the world. In rebuttal I would say that the white people are the only people that are the hope of the world, because they are the only people who

The Address-Mr. Thomas have solved the difficult problem of production and the method of distributing the surplus of their production to other people of the world. How are people to be fed unless some civilization solves the production problem? I would say that the coloured people can look to the white people for their idealism and to safeguard them and lead them to a better life rather than look to those nations that would destroy not only them but us.
The science of destruction has advanced rapidly throughout all the world. It is the prayer of all good men that this same science, energy, striving for peace, brains and money could be utilized to eliminate poverty and disease in the world, and that we endeavour to offer to all the people of the world, whatever their colour may be, our assistance in regard to their needs, physically, mentally and psychologically.
I am sure that Canadians will accept their responsibility along with the other twelve nations of the United Nations Organization, first to maintain peace, second, to guarantee that peace in the present-day world by being strong, and third, to recognize with all of the people on earth their right, along with ours, to health, wealth and happiness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal during the course of this debate about whether or not war with the Soviet union is inevitable. We certainly hope that it is not. But war will be inevitable if we fail to make our forces strong enough to defeat the forces of communism.
There is no way on this earth that we can talk to them, get together with them and form any compromise. Stalin has made it clear on many occasions that they are out to rule the world, and nothing short of that will be satisfactory. That end has been advocated all the way down from the time of Marx, and it will never change. The Russian minister of education as quoted in the September issue of Outlook said-I will not attempt to give the exact words, but the effect of his statement was this: "We must hate Christians. Even the best Christian is our worst enemy. They preach the doctrine, love thy neighbour. We say, hate thy neighbour; for without hate we cannot conquer the world". These are the men, Mr. Speaker, that we are trying to talk to and attempting to pacify. It simply cannot be done, and the only possible way that we can stop this Russian aggression is by seeing that we are willing not only to match their strength but to go beyond it. We must remember also that now we have not only Russia to deal with,


but practically all of the Orient. We can blame ourselves for the fact that the Chinese people's government has lined itself alongside Russia.
I am mighty glad to see the Colombo plan going ahead. It will be a good thing, but it should have been done fifteen or twenty years ago. Those people were starving; they have been starving for years while we in the so-called western democratic countries have been crying because we had surpluses and no markets in which to place them. We made it evident to them that the only interest we had in their affairs was that of exploitation. Now, twenty years too late, we are trying to give some aid to those undeveloped countries. Years ago we should have shown that we have some sense of responsibility and some thought in line with that, spirit of Christian charity about which we boast so often. Now, after all these years, when it is too late, we offer them assistance-not through the goodness of our hearts but through the fear of communism.
According to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) the defence of Canada is to be the first consideration. I agree wholeheartedly; but for goodness' sake let us go ahead and do something. Reports indicate that voluntary enlistments in the armed forces are not sufficient, that the permanent army is about seven thousand below required strength and that the reserves are greatly undermanned. Surely, if the minister says that the defence of Canada is our first consideration, we should do something about the deficiencies in our reserve army at least.
Many people say that compulsory service in the reserve force would withdraw men from the active army to serve in the capacity of instructors. That is not so. There are any number of good officers, retired and medically unfit for active service who, if asked, would be only too willing to give their service for the training of these men.
As a matter of fact during the last war the thirty-day training schools were staffed almost one hundred per cent by men medically unfit for the active armies. I would be the first to admit that most communities have inadequate facilities and equipment to go into a large scale training plan at the present time. But, after all, whose responsibility is that? Why do they not have the equipment and facilities they need? While much of it may be out of date, we have now enough equipment at least to make a beginning.
Speaking the other day the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said that

at present in the reserve forces we find parades called with only about six officers and four men showing up. That is in itself sufficient reason to see that these reserve training units should be brought up to capacity. Quite apart from war, this military training would not do anyone any harm, especially the youngsters. It gives an opportunity for first-class physical training for those who need it. As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) pointed out last night, at least it teaches those who attend which end of the gun to hold to their shoulder before pulling the trigger.
There is no doubt that in the present situation compulsory training is essential. Let us have cadet training in the schools and colleges. Let the young men have their training, and then permit them to go into industry, with the understanding that they may come back one or two evenings each week to gain at least some knowledge of any technological advances there may have been.
With respect to registration: if war were to come to Canada we would find registration absolutely essential. The present outlook indicates that such a thing might happen in a very short time. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, speaking the other day, threw a challenge across the floor of the house in which he asked the opposition how to save money. If the government wants to save money, then let it have the registration made at the same time the census is taken next summer. By doing that they would see how many millions in expenses they could save.
National registration would give the government an idea as to the possibilities of each and every person in the country, and also a very clear indication of any subversive elements we may have-and believe me we have some. That, too, is our own fault. We have those subversive elements here today because the government has refused time and again to put forth some sort of concrete financial policy which would offer the people of Canada some degree of security.
We won the last war, but not necessarily because the men and machines we had were better than those possessed by the Germans. I would be the first to say that the Canadian armed forces were the best to be found anywhere in the world. But we won that war simply because we had more men and equipment than did our enemy. Then, let us get ahead, and see that we have more equipment this time-because if war comes we are going to need it, and need it badly.
The Address-Mr. Thomas Speaking the other day, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) said that American forces were going into Korea after eighteen-day refresher courses. We do not want to see that happen here. My mind goes back to the early days of the last war, when men had to be sent across with no knowledge at all of military affairs. This time we may not have a buffer state to protect us until our men are ready. Not only that, we have no reason to believe that we might not be attacked right here on our own soil. It was reported in the press not long ago that one of the United States pilots in Korea had stated that if the United States had had the MIG-15 jet plane and if the communists in Korea had been equipped with the United States jet planes they would have been slaughtered, they would have wiped the skies with the North Korean communists. That bodes ill when you consider that for the most part the Chinese communist pilots are poorly trained. What would happen if we were to run into superior numbers of well-trained Russian pilots in their apparently superior MIG-15 fighter planes? While I am speaking about jet planes and pilots I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of February 8 which reads:
400 jets a month said Russian aim
Russia is expanding production of her MIG-15 jet fighter planes and, say Swedish sources, expects to be producing 400 a month in the next few months, the magazine Aviation Age said yesterday. It said American production of planes of all types does not exceed 250 a month.
That means that our whole defence program is entirely inadequate, not only in connection with the training of men for the reserve and active forces but in connection with our industries. There is already a shortage of manpower, and training in the reserve forces is the only way this country can have its men trained without disrupting industry. If the government want to get manpower all .they need to do is to remove the means test from the veterans allowances and the old age pensions. They will find that these older people can do a good job. They may not be able to do the hard work that younger men can do but there are many jobs in industry they can handle quite well.
Let us call upon the women of this country. They will go into industry if required. Let us encourage the married women to go to work by allowing them to earn up to the income tax exemption of a single person without any penalty being imposed upon the husband. There is really no shortage of manpower in Canada. We have lots of it if the government will go ahead and utilize what is available. These things will create

The Address-Mr. Thomas small inconveniences, and I think that is admitted by all. But will anyone in this house say that a few inconveniences are not better than slavery under the heel of Moscow?
Accusations have been flying around the house ever since this debate started about skating around this and skating around that. The official opposition has accused the government of skating around the international situation and not giving the people a true picture. The government has accused the official opposition of skating around by not making any concrete proposals. The C.C.F. has accused the government of skating around something else. Incidentally the best job of skating around I have seen was the speech this afternoon of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). He made the best Liberal speech
I have ever heard in this house. If skating is a good description to use, I think the floor of this House of Commons during this debate would remind me of a community skating rink on a Sunday afternoon when the subject of manpower is mentioned.
To carry on just a bit further with this skating, this amendment has the effect of giving members of this house and those who are doing so much skating, the rules of the game and a hockey stick. Let us get on with the game.
